experience_thesis: A public-document-based marketplace and experience-design lens on customer desire, trust between strangers, design as a way systems work, and founder attention to product details, based on Airbnb public materials and interviews.

principles.statement: Design the whole service system, not just its visual interface; include the operational and trust mechanisms required for the promised experience to work.
limitations: Airbnb's marketplace model has distinctive trust, regulatory and supply-side characteristics.
Design quality cannot compensate for weak unit economics or poor service delivery.

principles.statement: Start with a customer problem people genuinely want solved, then use customer response and word of mouth as signals of product value.
limitations: Customer enthusiasm must be validated through retention, repeat use, willingness to pay and contribution economics.
Anecdotes about early adoption do not establish scalable demand.

principles.statement: For marketplaces involving strangers, trust is a core product capability that must be deliberately designed into the experience.
limitations: Trust mechanisms need to be tailored to local law, safety, fraud patterns and marketplace category.
Identity checks, reviews and guarantees can create privacy, bias and operational trade-offs.

principles.statement: Maintain founder attention on product details and the end-to-end customer experience while avoiding confusing detail orientation with unstructured micromanagement.
limitations: Founder involvement must evolve with organisational scale and management capability.
Centralised design decisions can slow teams or suppress local insight if poorly governed.

decision_cases.title: Treating Airbnb's trust system as part of product design
decision_cases.context: In a 2020 Airbnb statement, Chesky described design as encompassing how the service fundamentally works, including the original business model and system of trust.
decision_cases.decision: Apply design thinking to the marketplace's operating model and trust infrastructure, not only its interface and aesthetics.
decision_cases.outcome: Airbnb's leadership materials describe a design-driven approach and trust system supporting a global host-guest marketplace. Scale figures are company-reported and do not establish causal attribution to design alone.
limitations: The public sources describe Airbnb's own philosophy and should not be treated as independent proof of causal impact.
Trust systems may create new costs, exclusion risks and regulatory obligations.

sources.title: Designing the Future of Airbnb
sources.notes: Statement by co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky describing design as how a system fundamentally works, including Airbnb's business model and trust system.

sources.title: Brian Chesky — Airbnb Executive Management
sources.notes: Official leadership biography describing the company's design-driven approach and trust system.

sources.title: Q&A with Brian Chesky, Co-Founder and CEO, Airbnb
sources.notes: Interview with Chesky about Airbnb's origin, customer desire, leadership and attention to operating details.

counter_evidence: Airbnb's growth has also involved market timing, network effects, capital, brand, supply acquisition and regulatory conditions; design alone cannot explain its outcomes.
Marketplace trust mechanisms can fail and may produce safety, discrimination, privacy and regulatory harms.
Founder-led attention to detail can become a bottleneck if not translated into clear decision rights and operating mechanisms.
transfer_conditions: Map trust requirements across onboarding, identity, payment, fulfilment, dispute resolution and safety.
Measure marketplace liquidity, repeat transactions, service quality, fraud, cancellation and contribution margin.
Test both sides of the marketplace; buyer demand without reliable supply (or vice versa) is insufficient.
Localise trust and compliance systems to each geography and category.
limitations: Public company statements and interviews only; no private thoughts or undocumented decisions.
